growth_story.headline: Colombia's oil-fuelled run of 2003-2014 gave way to a decade of 1.2 percent growth in income per person, with investment now far below its 2015 level.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2002 income per person grew only 0.9 percent a year, and the era ended in the 1999 crisis, when it fell 5.9 percent. From 2003 to 2014 growth rose to 3.5 percent a year: an opening of the oil sector let Colombia ride a long rise in oil prices, and more people took jobs, many of them formal. Since 2015 growth has averaged 1.3 percent a year, and the IMF ties the turn to a sharp and largely lasting fall in oil and other commodity prices from 2014, after which investment slowed and then fell. The pandemic brought a fall of 8.5 percent in 2020 and rebounds of 9.6 in 2021 and 6.2 in 2022, but growth then slipped to -0.3 in 2023, 0.4 in 2024 and 1.6 in 2025. Investment fell from 23.4 percent of GDP in 2015 to 16.0 in 2025, and the World Bank describes a recovery carried by demand and public spending while productivity stalls and the room in the budget shrinks. Income per person reached a new high in 2025, but the last decade's 1.2 percent average is far below the 3.5 of the decade before.

threads.title: Oil opening and price boom
threads.text: In 2003 Colombia opened up and restructured its oil sector, and as oil prices boomed, oil output roughly doubled. More people joined the workforce and moved into formal jobs, which also lifted growth in the 2003-2014 era.

citations.title: Potential Growth in Colombia (IMF Working Paper WP/17/238)
citations.quote: In 2003, Colombia liberalized and restructured the oil sector, modifying the contract and taxation frameworks

citations.title: Potential Growth in Colombia (IMF Working Paper WP/17/238)
citations.quote: A liberalization of the oil sector allowed the country to further take advantage of the oil price boom, by roughly doubling oil production

citations.title: Potential Growth in Colombia (IMF Working Paper WP/17/238)
citations.quote: A large increase in labor participation and formalization also supported this growth acceleration

threads.title: The 2014 oil price collapse
threads.text: Oil prices fell sharply from 2014, and the IMF judged most of the fall to be lasting. Investment slowed markedly and fell in 2016, which marks the turn to the slower era that began in 2015.

citations.title: Potential Growth in Colombia (IMF Working Paper WP/17/238)
citations.quote: In contrast, the sharp and largely permanent decline in oil and other commodity prices since 2014 have taken a toll on growth.

citations.title: Potential Growth in Colombia (IMF Working Paper WP/17/238)
citations.quote: Investment decelerated markedly and even declined in 2016, as oil prices more than halved and trading partner growth turned negative.

citations.title: IMF Survey: Drop in Oil Prices Poses Challenges for Colombia
citations.quote: The sharp drop in oil prices poses significant challenges to Colombia’s near-term outlook.

threads.title: Investment below pre-pandemic levels
threads.text: Investment fell from 23.4 percent of GDP in 2015 to 16.0 in 2025. The World Bank says the recovery after the pandemic leaned on demand and public spending, and the IMF points to uncertainty about policies and reforms as something that could hold back investment further.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Colombia (October 2026)
citations.quote: Growth has relied on demand and fiscal support, while investment remains below pre-pandemic levels and foreign direct investments (FDI) fell to 15-year lows.

citations.title: IMF Staff Completes Article IV Mission to Colombia
citations.quote: Domestic uncertainty around implementation of policies and reforms could further hold back investment.

threads.title: A shrinking fiscal cushion
threads.text: Weak revenues and rigid spending have eaten into the room in the budget. In 2025 the government suspended its fiscal rule through 2027, and the country's credit rating was then cut.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Colombia (October 2026)
citations.quote: Weak revenues, rigid spending, and energy-transition pressures have eroded fiscal space, triggering the fiscal rule suspension and subsequent sovereign downgrades.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2025 Article IV Consultation with Colombia
citations.quote: The government invoked the escape clause to suspend the fiscal rule through 2027.

threads.title: Stalled productivity, commodity exports
threads.text: The World Bank describes productivity that has stagnated and exports still concentrated in commodities. It says this has slowed Colombia's catch-up with richer countries.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Colombia (April 2026)
citations.quote: However, productivity has stagnated, slowing income convergence and gains in poverty and inequality reduction.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Colombia (April 2026)
citations.quote: Limited global integration constrains diversification beyond commodities.

since_last_year.text: Growth picked up in 2025 and early 2026 on consumption and public spending. In 2026 the Chocó earthquake added reconstruction costs to an already strained budget, a new government took office, and the World Bank now expects growth to slow in 2026.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Colombia (October 2026)
citations.quote: Growth is projected at 2.3 percent in 2026, from 2.6 percent in 2025, as the Chocó earthquake compounds pre-existing fiscal fragility.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Colombia (October 2026)
citations.quote: Real GDP growth accelerated to 2.9 percent in 2026H1, from 2.6 percent in 2025, on stronger-than-expected consumption.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Colombia (October 2026)
citations.quote: The new government inherits a demanding agenda: restoring fiscal credibility and stabilizing debt

growth_story.tension: The sources describe growth picking up in 2025 on strong consumption, but income per person rose only 1.6 percent that year. The gap is population growth: part of the headline gain went to a larger population rather than higher incomes. Income per person is at a record in 2025, yet it is little above where it stood in 2022.
